definition: Anthology means a collection of selected writings, poems, or songs by various authors, published together.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word anthology. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know anthology should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: For her brother's birthday, Amara chose an anthology of science-fiction stories, so he could sample twelve different writers in a single book.
A sampler offers just a few short pieces to give readers a quick taste — slimmer than an anthology, which brings together a full selection of writings by many authors.
A compendium goes further than an anthology: it tries to gather everything important on a subject in exhaustive detail, not just a chosen selection.

Collection is the broadest word for works gathered together — one author's essays, one museum's paintings, anything assembled at all. An anthology is a specific kind of collection: selected writings by many different authors, published together in one volume. Every anthology is a collection; a collection needs no variety of voices.

Compilation stresses the labor of assembling material from many sources, and the material can be anything — statistics, film clips, songs. An anthology is narrower: a published volume of selected writings by various authors. Call the spreadsheet of election results a compilation; call the book of thirty writers' stories an anthology.

Treasury presents gathered works as precious — a treasury of verse promises gems worth keeping. An anthology makes no claim about value; it is simply selected writings by various authors published in one volume. Treasury adds a tone of celebration that a plain classroom anthology does not carry.

When the city library lost half its poetry shelf to a burst pipe, the head librarian saw a chance rather than a loss.
Instead of replacing every slim volume, she ordered a single fat anthology of twentieth-century poems.
One book now held a hundred and four poets — famous names beside writers few patrons had ever met.
Circulation of poetry tripled within a year.
Readers who came for one poet kept turning pages and left having discovered three more.
Purists grumbled that a poet deserves a whole book.
The librarian's answer stayed the same: a reader who meets a poet in a shared volume can always go looking for more.
